subjects.label: Jesus
subjects.summary: Matthew and Luke place Jesus at the centre of their birth narratives.

subjects.label: The Magi's visit
subjects.summary: Matthew's Magi enter a house and see the child with Mary. No exact interval from the birth is stated.

subjects.label: The flight to Egypt
subjects.summary: Matthew narrates Joseph taking the child and Mary to Egypt after a warning.

subjects.label: The return to Nazareth
subjects.summary: Matthew narrates a return after Herod's death; Luke closes the presentation account with a return to Nazareth. Their sequences need separate reading.

subjects.label: Quirinius' assessment of Judaea
subjects.summary: Josephus describes an assessment following Archelaus' removal. Its usual AD 6 dating creates a difficulty for combining Luke 2 with Herod's reign.

subjects.label: Herod's death
subjects.summary: Josephus' regnal totals and eclipse narrative underpin competing reconstructions of Herod's death.

subjects.label: December 25 in the Chronography of 354
subjects.summary: The fourth-century calendar places Christ's birth at Bethlehem on December 25.

subjects.label: March Jupiter occultation
subjects.summary: The existing calculation record places a lunar occultation of Jupiter on 20 March 6 BC, proleptic Julian. This doesn't identify a birth.

subjects.label: September sky proposal
subjects.summary: Martin interprets a September evening through Revelation 12; the existing calculations examine positions and setting times, not the birth itself.

subjects.label: Spring equinox in 6 BC
subjects.summary: The existing calculations place the equinox on 23 March 6 BC Julian, equivalent to 21 March Gregorian.

dateModels.label: Birth around 6–4 BC
assumptions: Matthew's birth precedes Herod's death.
Use the conventional 4 BC death framework.
6–4 BC is a practical historical range; its early boundary is not a direct biblical date.
Month and day remain unknown.
dateModels.strength: A pre-Herod-death setting consistent with Matthew.
objections: Luke's Quirinius reference remains unresolved.
Herod's death alone supplies a latest limit, not the entire range.

dateModels.label: 20 March 6 BC
assumptions: Use the early Molnar/Cahn version.
Interpret the occultation as a royal sign linked specifically to Jesus.
A Nisan 1 identification needs a separate historical calendar argument.
dateModels.strength: An astronomical candidate within the proposed 6–4 BC range.
objections: It isn't the spring equinox on that calendar.
Molnar's later proposal favoured 17 April.
No surviving Magi record identifies this event as Jesus' birth.

dateModels.label: 11 September 3 BC
assumptions: Read Revelation 12 as a dateable sky description.
Adopt a Herod chronology that permits a 3 BC birth.
Identify this evening with the birth and, separately, Tishri 1.
dateModels.strength: A specific interpretation whose astronomical component can be checked.
objections: Revelation doesn't name Virgo or a birthday.
Requires moving Herod's death later than 4 BC.
Existing calculations give about 42 minutes from sunset to moonset near Jerusalem, not Martin's 90.

dateModels.label: 25 December
assumptions: Distinguish the attested commemoration from a proposed historical birthday.
No birth year follows from the annual date alone.
objections: No demonstrated independent chain from the calendar entry to the original birth.
Later calculation and historical memory remain alternatives.

dateModels.label: Autumn service → winter birth
assumptions: Assume service and John's conception in September/October of year A.
Add roughly six months to Jesus' conception and roughly nine to his birth.
These starting months are examples, not recovered Abijah service dates.
dateModels.strength: Demonstrates the remembered winter route coherently.
objections: The service-cycle anchor is missing.
Luke's sixth month isn't an exact elapsed six-month interval.
The annual high-priestly rite doesn't follow from Luke's incense scene.

dateModels.label: Spring service → summer birth
assumptions: Assume service and John's conception in March/April of year A.
Use the same approximate conception and pregnancy intervals.
dateModels.strength: Shows why choosing a different service turn changes the outcome.
objections: No securely dated service occurrence selects this route.
A continuous 24-week rotation is 168 days, not exactly six calendar months.

dateModels.label: Historical context
assumptions: AD 6 for Quirinius' assessment.
4 BC as the conventional Herod death year.
objections: Herod's minority alternative is retained separately.
An earlier enrollment isn't established by this record.

dateModels.label: Existing astronomical checks
assumptions: Use the recorded observer near Jerusalem.
Regular proleptic calendars; ideal horizon and model refraction.
No inferred Nisan/Tishri dates or ancient visibility claim.
objections: Prior results imported; ephemerides weren't rerun here.
A calculated sky doesn't establish an ancient interpretation or birth.

dateModels.label: Narrative order; absolute dates unknown
assumptions: Keep each Gospel's sequence attributed to that Gospel.
Do not create a detailed combined itinerary.
dateModels.strength: Allows exploration without guessing a birthday.
objections: Relative order leaves many durations unknown.

dateModels.label: Fourth-century calendar witness
assumptions: Date the surviving compilation rather than the birth from its annual entry.
objections: Not an eyewitness account of the nativity.
